draft.title: Modality
card: Modality is the strength of a writer's certainty, or of the force of a demand. Modal words show it.
strong words such as must, will, certainly and always. They sound sure or forceful, as in "Schools must ban phones".
weaker words such as might, could, perhaps and sometimes. They sound unsure or gentle, as in "Schools could ban phones".
Words such as should and probably sit in the middle. A writer picks modal words to push a reader hard or to leave room for other views.
draft.remember: Modal words set how sure or forceful a writer sounds, from high to low.

a.q: Which sentence uses the highest modality?
opts: Every student must join the clean-up day
Every student should join the clean-up day
Every student could join the clean-up day
Every student might join the clean-up day
a.why: Must is the strongest modal word here, so it sounds the most forceful. Should is tempting, but it is a medium word and leaves more room to say no.
a.clue: Which word leaves the reader no choice?

b.q: Ravi writes: "The new bus route might help some families." What effect does the modality have?
opts: It sounds cautious and unsure about the benefit
It sounds forceful and demands action from readers
It sounds certain that every family will benefit
It sounds angry and blames the council for delays
b.why: Might and some are low modality, so the claim is tentative. It is not forceful, because a writer who was demanding action would use words such as must or will.
b.clue: Look at might and some, then ask how sure they sound.

a.best: Every student must join the clean-up day

b.best: It sounds cautious and unsure about the benefit

problems.detail: The why says 'Might and some are low modality', and the clue points to 'some' as a modal word. 'Some' is a quantifier that limits the claim; it is not a modal word, and the card never presents it as one. Only 'might' carries the modality here. Reword so 'some' is described as narrowing or hedging the claim, not as modality.
